title: October deliberations show why Canada raised rates while core inflation was still near 2%
summary: On 28 October Governing Council raised the overnight rate by a quarter point to 2.5%. The account published on 10 November shows that the choice was between that increase and a hold at 2.25%. Both options were argued on the basis of evidence already available. Excluding gasoline, inflation was 2.2%, core measures remained near 2% and the share of components rising at least 3% was near its historical average. The reason for acting was a forward-looking change. An energy shock treated as an adverse scenario in April had become part of the central projection, and stronger growth would gradually remove the slack that had constrained firms’ pricing power (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Policy decision).

The oil benchmark was roughly US$35 per barrel above the level assumed in the July Report. Both the level of the futures curve and the time for which markets expected high prices had risen. Restrictions on Middle Eastern supplies and strained refining capacity kept gasoline, diesel and heating oil expensive. Council judged direct energy effects alone could leave CPI around 3% for more than a year, even if firms did not pass additional input costs through. The new projection went further: it put inflation at 3½% by end-2026, above 3% through much of 2027 and back at 2% only by mid-2028. These are conditional forecast values, not the observed inflation rate at publication. The longer implied period above target changed the risk to expectations (International economy and Considerations for monetary policy).

Surveyed firms had absorbed much of the cost so far but expected to pass a greater share on over the next year. The list of costs had expanded beyond fuel. Chemicals, plastics and rubber embodied oil costs; imported semiconductors and computer components were becoming dearer as AI investment ran into supply constraints. An increase in transport costs alone might remain visible mostly in airline tickets and petrol. Repeated increases in intermediate and imported goods could travel through several production and distribution stages, reaching customers later. Members agreed on the likely direction of this process and differed about its speed and extent. Near-term inflation expectations had risen. Longer-term measures remained anchored, with households’ and firms’ responses to recent price changes potentially affected by the pandemic-era inflation experience (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

Output was also supplying less protection against higher inflation. GDP rose 3.3% in the second quarter and indicators pointed to about 2% in the third. The second was a contemporary estimate. New US trade actions were expected to weigh on fourth-quarter activity. Yet consumer spending per person was rising, supported by labour income and wealth. Energy and other goods exports had improved, with additional pipeline capacity and US demand expected to help even as tariffs hurt affected products. Council lifted its 2026 growth projection to 1% and expected 2% in 2027 and 2028. It still saw excess supply but expected it to be absorbed progressively. A growth upgrade can therefore raise projected pass-through even if the economy has not yet reached capacity (Canadian economy and inflation outlook).

The investment outlook was uneven. Energy prices supported oil and gas capital spending, firms were investing in AI and government incentives and major projects could encourage investment. Even with a pickup, investment as a share of GDP was still low relative to history, and uncertainty about trade could delay projects. Residential investment was expected to remain weak owing to affordability, demographics, higher mortgage rates and uncertainty. Labour conditions were broadly sideways. Unemployment was around 6½%, public employment had fallen, and private-sector employment was relatively resilient. Some members read the private-sector evidence as indicating a stronger labour market than aggregate figures alone suggested. Others continued to emphasise slack and weaker sentiment among firms surveyed after trade talks broke down (Canadian economy and inflation outlook and Policy decision).

Global demand had been more resilient than July’s projection as US and Asian AI investment expanded, while high energy costs weighed on importers including the euro area. Global growth was expected to stabilise around 3%. Sovereign yields rose through both policy expectations and term premia. Canadian yields rose less than US yields, while the Canadian dollar had broadly returned to the level used in the July projection after earlier depreciation. Equity volatility reflected concerns about the durability of AI earnings. These market developments could affect financing and import costs, but the summary does not identify an announcement-day surprise or an asset return attributable to the Canadian decision (International economy).

The case for a hold centred on observed breadth, available slack and new tariffs. The case for a hike centred on accumulating costs, intentions to reprice and shrinking downside growth risks. Council judged that waiting for the core measures to turn might allow higher fuel costs to become more generalised. A higher overnight rate could restrain that propagation through domestic demand and expectations even though it could not lower international energy prices. The account gives no numerical division of votes and sets no prearranged sequence of increases. Members acknowledged that another increase might be needed, but retained a meeting-by-meeting approach in view of uncertainty about energy, Canada–US trade, financial conditions and firms’ responses. The relevant next data point was therefore the pattern of price changes alongside growth, rather than any single crude-oil or CPI threshold (Considerations for monetary policy and Policy decision).

questions.question: Did firms expecting to pass on costs actually reprice over the following year?
questions.detail: Connect original-vintage survey responses to later selling prices and margins, separating energy-based inputs, imported technology and domestically supplied services. Include measures of sales and customer retention. Larger rises among firms with recovering demand and persistent costs would support the feedback Council expected. A change in firms’ intended pricing alone would remain weaker evidence than realised changes in transactions.

questions.question: Was the projected absorption of slack broad enough to alter the pricing environment?
questions.detail: Follow employment, hours, hiring rates and wages in private and public sectors separately. Compare energy-exposed regions and construction or technology firms with tariff-affected manufacturing and housing. Record initial estimates and revisions to third-quarter growth. A concentrated rise in export earnings or a transfer from public to private employment could change the aggregate data without giving most firms stronger pricing power.

questions.question: How much of the policy-path revision was already priced before the October decision?
questions.detail: Reconstruct expectations for the current and subsequent meetings before the 28 October announcement and the simultaneous Report. Measure the separate response on 10 November when the deliberations became public. Control for changes in oil, refining margins, US rates and the Canadian dollar. A move in longer bond yields can reflect a term premium or global news as well as a changed Canadian rate path.
